Fulfilling a customer's order › Stage 2: Accept the order

Alerts proposed: Accept the order

Each is its own alert. When one fires, follow its own entry in the runbook. Thresholds, windows and whether an alert pages a person are the operators’ values, not set here.

Orders past the acceptance promise, by state

Its entry in the runbook ›

The question it answersHow many orders have waited longer than the promise to be accepted, and in which state are they held?
What it counts

SELECT "OrderStatus", count(*) FROM ordering.orders WHERE "OrderStatus" IN ('Submitted','AwaitingValidation','StockConfirmed') AND now() - "OrderDate" > interval '2 minutes' GROUP BY 1 (the interval is the stage's proposed promise); in the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run psql -U postgres -d orderingdb

Counted on cases.

Why it is proposedan order still in Submitted, AwaitingValidation or StockConfirmed past the promise has not been accepted when the shopper expects, and the moves out of AwaitingValidation and StockConfirmed strand it with nothing to move it again (lifecycle “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order”, “The order is cancelled because an item is out of stock”, “Payment is taken for the order” and “The order is cancelled because payment failed”, recovery stranded)
Which cases its entry worksBy the state the case is in: Submitted, AwaitingValidation, StockConfirmed. Its runbook entry groups the cases by state and works each state's tests.
ThresholdOperator value, not set here. For each measure, the value at which the alert fires. Whether it pages a person, opens a ticket or shows on a dashboard is the operators' decision.
WindowOperator value, not set here. How long the condition must hold before it fires. What the design assumes about time: Grace period GracePeriodTime 1 minute, polled every CheckUpdateTime 30 seconds. Every run re-publishes for each order still Submitted. The bus's retry policy never retries a failed publish: Execute is given an async lambda, so the failure lands in the returned task, not the call; 10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set. Ordering API consumes its queue with one consumer on one channel, so these waits queue behind one another; 10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set, queued behind the other waits as in “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order”; 10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set, on the same single consumer as “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order”.
Age boundOperator value. The stage’s promise: proposed: 2 minutes from entering Submitted, read from the timing of “The order is released for stock checking when the grace period ends”, “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order” and “Payment is taken for the order”: a 1-minute grace period and up to 30 seconds to the next poll, then 10 seconds before StockConfirmed and 10 before Paid. The stage is entered when the record is created, so a case's age in it is now minus "OrderDate"
No dataIt also fires when its measure cannot be counted for longer than the window. A count that finds no events in a window is zero, not missing data. A count fails when what it is read from is down; What it counts says where that is.
Symptom, not causeIt fires on what happens to cases, not on any component’s errors. Telling causes apart is the runbook’s job.
Exists todayno, proposed
For maintainers: register ids and sources

  • Basis as written: yes: an order still in Submitted, AwaitingValidation or StockConfirmed past the promise has not been accepted when the shopper expects, and the moves out of AwaitingValidation and StockConfirmed strand it with nothing to move it again (lifecycle L04-L07, recovery stranded)

Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed

Its entry in the runbook ›

The question it answersHow many orders entering acceptance are cancelled because payment failed?
What it counts

Ordering-api log lines 'Handling integration event:' naming OrderPaymentFailedIntegrationEvent, one per order, searched over the window in the log store, against the orders that entered acceptance in it ("OrderDate" in ordering.orders)

Counted on cases.

Why it is proposeda payment outage cancels every order that reaches StockConfirmed (“The order is cancelled because payment failed”), and none of them waits, so “Orders past the acceptance promise, by state” stays flat while the shopper loses the order
Which cases its entry worksBy the move the case left by: “The order is cancelled because payment failed” from StockConfirmed. Its runbook entry works that state's tests.
ThresholdOperator value, not set here. For each measure, the value at which the alert fires. Whether it pages a person, opens a ticket or shows on a dashboard is the operators' decision.
WindowOperator value, not set here. How long the condition must hold before it fires. What the design assumes about time: Grace period GracePeriodTime 1 minute, polled every CheckUpdateTime 30 seconds. Every run re-publishes for each order still Submitted. The bus's retry policy never retries a failed publish: Execute is given an async lambda, so the failure lands in the returned task, not the call; 10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set. Ordering API consumes its queue with one consumer on one channel, so these waits queue behind one another; 10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set, queued behind the other waits as in “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order”; 10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set, on the same single consumer as “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order”.

Companion measures

Read by the runbook’s checks, not proposed for alerting:

  • Grace-period releases published
  • Order Processor exits and restarts
  • Grace-period poll query failures
  • Grace period and poll interval in effect
  • Event bus start failures
  • Bindings on exchange eshop_event_bus
  • Queue Ordering: messages waiting and consumers
  • Ordering API messages it failed to handle
  • Ordering API messages of an event type it does not know
  • Ordering API transaction failures, by command
  • Ordering database accepting connections
  • Long-running statements on orderingdb
  • Connections to the postgres server against max_connections
  • Broker running
  • Broker resource alarms and headroom
  • Ordering outbox rows not published, by State
  • Ordering API publish failures
  • Catalog outbox rows by State
  • Catalog API publish failures
  • Payment Processor messages it failed to handle
  • Payment results published, by kind
  • Queue Catalog: messages waiting and consumers
  • Queue PaymentProcessor: messages waiting and consumers
  • Catalog API messages it failed to handle
  • Catalog database accepting connections
  • Long-running statements on catalogdb
  • Connections to the postgres server from catalogdb
